segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as for you, speak what is fitting for sound teaching.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Older men are to be sober, dignified, sensible, sound in faith, in love, and in endurance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Older women likewise are to be reverent in their bearing, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teachers of what is good,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that they may teach the young women good sense—to love their husbands and their children,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to be sensible, pure, busy at home, kind, submitting to their own husbands, so that the word of God may not be slandered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Likewise urge the younger men to be sensible.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In everything show yourself a model of good works: in your teaching, integrity, dignity,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and sound speech that is beyond reproach, so that the opponent may be put to shame, having nothing bad to say about us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be pleasing to them, not talking back,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not pilfering, but showing complete and genuine faithfulness, so that in everything they may adorn the teaching of God our Savior.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires and to live sensibly, justly, and with godliness in the present age,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as we wait for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people of his own, eager for good works.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Speak these things, and urge and rebuke with full authority. Let no one disregard you.

notes.note: This word family runs through the chapter (verses 2, 4, 5, 6 and 12) and is rendered with “sensible,” “good sense” and “sensibly” so the repetition can be heard. It named a prized Greek virtue: sound judgment that keeps impulses in check. Many versions use “self-controlled,” which is a fair gloss but is also the usual rendering of a different Greek word.

The adjective means “befitting what is sacred” and was used of people and conduct connected with temples and priestly service. The suggestion is that older women should carry themselves as people engaged in holy service.

The earliest manuscripts read a rare word meaning “working at home”; many later ones read a commoner word meaning “staying at home” or “keeping house,” which lies behind the King James “keepers at home.” The following adjective, “good,” is taken here as a separate quality (“kind”), but it can be joined to this word to give “good homemakers.”

The Greek verb meant defamatory speech against anyone or anything, not only irreverence toward God. Here the object is the Christian message, which outsiders would speak ill of if believers behaved badly, so “slandered” is used. Several versions keep “blasphemed” or use “reviled” or “maligned.” The “slanderers” of verse 3 translates a different Greek word.

notes.traditional: in all things shewing thyself a pattern
notes.note: The Greek phrase stands between the two sentences and could end verse 6 (“to be sensible in everything”) instead of beginning verse 7. The translation follows the punctuation of the Greek edition used and most English versions.

The word refers to people owned by a master, a normal part of households in the Roman world, and “servants” in older versions softens this. Most modern translations use “slaves.” The instruction addresses how believers in that position should act; it does not discuss the institution itself.

This is the same Greek word rendered “faith” in verse 2. Set against pilfering, it means the quality of being trustworthy, so “faithfulness” is used. The Greek is literally “showing all good faithfulness.”

The verb, and the related noun “appearing” in verse 13, were used in the Greek world for the visible manifestation of a god or the arrival of a ruler to help his people. The two occurrences frame the present life between Christ’s first appearing and his awaited one.

notes.traditional: that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men
notes.note: “To all people” can go either with “bringing salvation,” as here and in most modern versions, or with “has appeared,” as in the King James Version. The word order favors the first.

Greek has one word family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice). The adverb here describes conduct that is right and fair toward others, and “justly” is used. Most versions have “righteously” or “upright.”

notes.phrase: our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ
notes.traditional: the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ
notes.note: The Greek can be read as naming one person, Jesus Christ, who is called both God and Savior, or two, “the great God” and “our Savior Jesus Christ.” Most modern translations and grammarians favor the first because a single article governs both nouns and “God and Savior” was a set phrase in the period, but the second remains possible. A third view takes “Jesus Christ” as explaining “the glory” of God.

The phrase echoes the Greek Old Testament, where God calls Israel his special possession among all nations (for example Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 7:6). “Peculiar” in older English meant “belonging exclusively to,” not “odd.”

candidates.reason: The word family (σώφρων, σωφρονέω, σωφρονίζω, σωφρόνως, σωφροσύνη) recurs across the Pastorals and elsewhere, and versions vary among self-controlled, sensible, sober-minded and prudent, colliding with ἐγκράτεια.
Translators split between “doctrine” and “teaching,” and the word is frequent in the Pastorals alongside διδαχή.
Used of wives, slaves, citizens and believers across the letters; “submit,” “be subject” and “be subordinate” carry different tones and should not vary arbitrarily.
The εὐσέβεια family (with its opposite ἀσέβεια) is a key term in the Pastorals and 2 Peter, and “godliness,” “piety,” “devotion” and “reverence” all compete.
A technical term for Christ’s manifestation in the Pastorals and 2 Thessalonians that should be rendered uniformly and kept distinct from παρουσία.
